tutorials.title: Plan, prove and hand off a task with the CLI
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWeave CLI workflow: increment, claim, done and handoff
tutorials.summary: A real SpecWeave run in a disposable repository: create an increment, claim its task, prove it with tests, hand off, and pick up the next task in a clean clone.
tutorials.outcome: You see the whole loop once: the plan, the claim, the test evidence and the handoff all travel with the repository.

chapters.title: Pick up in a clean clone

steps: Create an increment with `specweave create-increment "title"`, then write the problem, the acceptance criteria and a task with its exact files and test command in spec.md.
Claim the task with `specweave task claim T-01`, so everyone can see who owns it.
Implement the change and run the tests. In the recording, both tests pass.
Commit, then run `specweave task done T-01 --run "<test command>"`. SpecWeave runs the command again and keeps its output as evidence.
Stop with `specweave handoff --reason "<why>"`. The recording keeps everything local instead of pushing.
In another clone, run `specweave pickup`. It prints the next task with its acceptance criteria.
tutorials.note: Actual CLI output from a disposable repository, SpecWeave 3.0.6: two passing tests, one of two tasks complete, and a local handoff into a clean clone. No remote push or production changes. AI narration in the author’s cloned voice; music: “Make Funk” by HoliznaCC0, CC0.

tutorials.title: Install SpecWeave and plan your first increment
tutorials.seoTitle: Install the SpecWeave CLI and plan your first increment
tutorials.summary: A real SpecWeave 3.1.0 run in a sample repo: npm i -g specweave, specweave init, specweave create-increment with a title, a filled-in spec.md with acceptance criteria, decisions and tasks, and specweave pickup naming the first task.
tutorials.outcome: You end with an increment whose spec.md lists numbered acceptance criteria and tasks with their files and test, and specweave pickup tells you which task to claim first.
prerequisites: a git repository to plan work in

chapters.title: Next: claim and prove the task

steps: Install the CLI with `npm i -g specweave`. It needs Node.js 20.12 or later; `specweave --version` prints the installed version.

In your repo, run `specweave init`. Add `--adapter claude` (or another tool) to name your coding agent, and `--quick` to accept the defaults. It writes CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, installs six SpecWeave skills in .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/, and keeps its settings in .specweave/config.json.
Run `specweave create-increment "Personal greeting"`. It creates .specweave/increments/0001-personal-greeting/ with a scaffolded spec.md and metadata.json.

Decide first: at the default level (`planning.deepInterview: critical`) your agent's sw-increment skill asks only the decisions that are yours, one at a time with a recommended answer, and records them under ## Decisions as Asked, Defaulted and Open.

Fill in spec.md, yourself or with the sw-increment skill: Problem, Scope, numbered acceptance criteria (`- [ ] AC-01: …`), Approach, Decisions, and tasks written as `### T-01 Title` followed by `- AC: AC-01 | Files: … | Test: …`.
Commit the plan and run `specweave pickup`. It prints the increment, the next task with its acceptance criterion, files and test, and the command that claims it.
Then claim the task with `specweave task claim T-01` and prove it with `specweave task done T-01 --run "npm test"`.
tutorials.note: Real output of the SpecWeave 3.1.0 CLI in a sample repo inside a disposable home, recorded headlessly. `npm i -g specweave` installed 3.1.0 from the npm registry into that home, and every later command ran the installed copy. No agent session is shown: the commands ran in a terminal with SPECWEAVE_TOOL=claude, which is why pickup reads claude@demo. The filled-in spec.md is a sample written in advance and swapped in for the scaffold off camera; no agent wrote it and no decisions were asked live. `--adapter claude` names the adapter so detection does not look at the recording machine's own tools. Nothing was pushed. Narration is an AI voice (ElevenLabs, the author's cloned voice); captions are timed from the voice service's character timestamps.

tutorials.title: Claim, prove, verify and complete a task
tutorials.seoTitle: Claim, prove, verify and complete a task with the SpecWeave CLI
tutorials.summary: A real SpecWeave 3.1.0 run in a sample repo: claim a task, prove it with task done --run and its evidence file, watch specweave complete refuse to close without a verify report, then run specweave verify and close the increment.
tutorials.outcome: You end with a completed increment that has its test evidence and a passing verify report.
prerequisites: SpecWeave installed with `npm i -g specweave` and a repo set up with `specweave init`
an increment whose spec.md lists a task with its acceptance criteria, Files and Test
steps: Claim the task with `specweave task claim T-01`. The claim goes into ledger.jsonl under your agent id (claude@demo in the recording), and the command prints the task's acceptance criteria, files and test. Another agent trying to claim it is refused while your claim is live.
Make the change and its test, and commit as `0001: <what changed>`.

Run `specweave task done T-01 --run "npm test"`. The test runs again; the task is marked done only when it exits 0, and the output is kept as evidence. A failing test exits 5 and the task is not marked done (the log is still saved).
Read the evidence file, reports/task-T-01.txt in the increment folder: the command, its exit code and the time, then the full test output.
`specweave complete 0001` refuses to close while reports/verify.json is missing, and tells you to run `specweave verify` first. Use `--reason` only if you must close without it.

Run `specweave verify`. It runs the verification commands (testing.commands in .specweave/config.json, otherwise the test, lint and build scripts from package.json) and counts an acceptance criterion as met when the tasks that cover it are done. It writes reports/verify.md and, beside it, reports/verify.json, which `specweave complete` reads.
Run `specweave complete 0001` again. The verify check passes and the increment's status becomes completed.
tutorials.note: Real output of the SpecWeave 3.1.0 CLI in a sample repo inside a disposable home, recorded headlessly. No agent session is shown: every command ran in a terminal with SPECWEAVE_TOOL=claude, which is how the ledger reads claude@demo. The change to src/greeting.js and its test were written off camera by the producer between the claim and task done, not by an agent; the change is shown as its real diff, and the video says so on the diff panel and the end card. The repo, spec and task are samples. Left out of the video: the 'Completing increment' line the blocked specweave complete prints before its error, the warnings both complete runs print (no review on file, no coverage data), and the empty Note cell of the verify report's task row. Nothing was pushed. Narration is an AI voice (ElevenLabs, the author's cloned voice); captions are timed from the voice service's character timestamps.

tutorials.title: Hand off from Claude Code to Codex at a usage limit
tutorials.seoTitle: Hand off from Claude Code to Codex at a usage limit with SpecWeave
tutorials.summary: A real SpecWeave 3.1.0 run in a sample repo: the usage guard warns at 95% of the 5-hour limit, specweave handoff writes handoff.md and releases the claim, and specweave pickup gives Codex the next task with its acceptance criteria. Codex proves the task with task done --run.
tutorials.outcome: You end with Codex running the next task from the ledger, and the ledger shows who handed off, who picked up and who finished.
prerequisites: SpecWeave installed with `npm i -g specweave` and a repo set up with `specweave init`
an increment whose spec.md lists tasks with their Files and Test

chapters.title: The next task and its acceptance criteria

steps: Turn on the usage guard once with `specweave auto-handoff on`. In the default suggest mode, the first time a session reaches 95% of a usage window it tells you a handoff is available and keeps working; nothing is said when every full window resets within 30 minutes.

When you decide to move, tell Claude Code to hand off. It runs `specweave handoff --reason "usage at 95% of the 5-hour limit"`, which releases its task claims and writes handoff.md and handoff.diff in the increment folder. With a Git remote it also pushes, so another machine can pick up.
Read handoff.md: who stopped and why, which tasks are done with their evidence, the uncommitted files with the full diff beside it, and the exact next step.
Open Codex in the same repo and say "pick up". Codex runs `specweave pickup`, which prints the next task with its acceptance criteria, files and test, and records a pickup line in ledger.jsonl.
Codex claims the task with `specweave task claim T-02` and makes the change.

Codex runs `specweave task done T-02 --run "npm test"`. The test runs again; the task is marked done only when it exits 0, and the ledger records who finished it, as codex@<host> (codex@demo in the recording), with the test output as evidence.
Then run `specweave verify` to check the increment before you close it with `specweave complete`.
tutorials.note: Real output of the SpecWeave 3.1.0 CLI in a sample repo inside a disposable home, recorded headlessly. Agent sessions are not shown: each command ran in a terminal as that agent (SPECWEAVE_TOOL=claude or codex), which is how the ledger reads claude@demo and codex@demo. The 95% usage reading is a sample passed to `specweave statusline` and `specweave usage-guard` in the format Claude Code sends; their output is real. The new T-02 test was written by Claude before the handoff (the uncommitted file in handoff.md); Codex's change to src/greeting.js was made off camera and is shown as its diff. Nothing was pushed. Narration is an AI voice (ElevenLabs, the author's cloned voice); captions are timed from the voice service's character timestamps.

tutorials.title: Review with the other model before you ship
tutorials.seoTitle: Review Claude Code's diff with Codex before you ship, with specweave review
tutorials.summary: A real SpecWeave 3.1.0 run in a sample repo: specweave review --brief shows what a reviewer gets, then specweave review sees in the ledger that Claude Code finished the task and has Codex, a model from another family, review the diff. Codex saves reports/review-codex.md with a high finding and the command exits 3. After the fix, a second review says ship and exits 0. In 3.1.0, as recorded, it overwrote the first report; from 3.1.1 each run keeps its own.
tutorials.outcome: You end with a review report from a model of another family and a clean second run.
prerequisites: SpecWeave installed with `npm i -g specweave` and a repo set up with `specweave init`
the Codex CLI installed and signed in (`codex login`)
an increment whose tasks are done on a branch, so there is a diff against main
steps: Finish the increment's tasks on a branch. The ledger records who finished each one (claude@demo in the recording).

Run `specweave review --brief` to see what the reviewer gets without running it: who wrote the code (counted from the ledger's done events), the acceptance criteria, the Approach, the tasks and the diff of the task files since the merge-base with main.

Run `specweave review`. It picks the first installed reviewer from another model family (Codex for code Claude wrote, Claude for code an OpenAI model wrote) and sends it that brief; Codex reviews it with `codex exec` in a read-only sandbox, using its own sign-in.
Read `reports/review-codex.md` in the increment folder. Every finding names a severity and a `path:line`. With any critical or high finding the verdict is `fix first` and `specweave review` exits 3.
Fix every critical and high finding (or add a task for it), run the tests, and commit.

Run `specweave review` again. With no critical or high finding left the verdict is `ship` and the exit code is 0. Each run appends a note to ledger.jsonl with the reviewer and its verdict, and `specweave pickup` shows the latest notes.

Each run keeps its own report in `reports/reviews/review-<reviewer>-<n>.md`, and `reports/review-<reviewer>.md` is always the latest; each ledger note names its own run's file. (In SpecWeave 3.1.0, as recorded, every run overwrote `reports/review-<reviewer>.md`; this changed in 3.1.1.)
Then run `specweave verify` and close the increment with `specweave complete`.
tutorials.note: Real output of the SpecWeave 3.1.0 CLI in a sample repo inside a disposable home, recorded headlessly. The review is a real Codex run: `specweave review` started codex-cli 0.162.1 with its built-in command (GPT-6.1-Sol, high reasoning, read-only sandbox); each review took about 30 seconds, and that wait is cut, with the verdict shown when it arrived. Agent sessions are not shown: the commands ran in a terminal as Claude Code (SPECWEAVE_TOOL=claude), which is how the ledger reads claude@demo. Claude Code's original change, its fix and the new test were scripted off camera for the demo and committed under the claude tool id; the video shows the fix commit with `git show`, and the end card says so. The brief, the fix commit and the overwritten report's verdict line were captured afterwards from the same disposable home, without running the reviewer. Some output is shortened on screen, marked with a dimmed …: the brief shows only its author, acceptance criteria and first diff hunk; the report's first line, an HTML comment with the reviewer, base and head commits and the time, is cut; the fix commit's file headers are cut; and the verdict lines show …/reports/review-codex.md instead of the absolute path into the disposable home. As the video says, the second review overwrote reports/review-codex.md, so the fix-first report the first ledger note names no longer exists (a SpecWeave 3.1.0 limitation fixed in 3.1.1, where each run keeps its own report under reports/reviews/). Nothing was pushed. Narration is an AI voice (ElevenLabs, the author's cloned voice); captions are timed from the voice service's character timestamps.

tutorials.title: See how SpecWithCode runs your agents
tutorials.seoTitle: How SpecWithCode works: machines, subscriptions, limits and threads
tutorials.summary: Each of your machines can hold several AI subscriptions, and every session runs on the machine itself. SpecWithCode connects the machines over Tailscale, watches every limit, and lets one coordinator per project start threads that open their own pull requests. Auto-resolve closes a thread only once it is merged, green and approved.
tutorials.outcome: You know how machines, subscriptions, usage limits, the coordinator and its threads fit together before you install.

chapters.title: More AI than you can use
Only one subscription? Pick its host

steps: Sign each machine in with the official tools. Keep every machine signed in to one account per provider for good, for example Claude Code on one account and Codex on another, and add machines when you need more capacity instead of switching subscriptions by hand.
If you have one subscription, run it on the machine with the most free memory and disk, because every session runs on that machine.
Connect your machines privately. Each machine runs its own SpecWithCode server.
Watch the limits: SpecWithCode shows session and weekly usage, banked resets and credits for every account. When one runs out, a thread waits for the reset or moves to another provider or machine.
In a project, talk to one coordinator. It plans, then starts threads for the work, each on the machine and model that fits, and each thread opens its own pull request.
Open a thread to see what it ran and what it is waiting on. A thread resolves itself only when its pull requests are merged, checks pass and the review is approved.
tutorials.note: Recorded on SpecWithCode 1.0.5 with the author's real EasyChamp project, 12 October 2026, through a read-only session; the thread pane is sped up 1.6x and hostnames are masked. Stock footage is from Pexels, the diagrams are animated, the music is AI-generated, and the narration is AI in the author's cloned voice. Since this recording, machines join over Tailscale with an invite line made in the app, and the other connection routes the video mentions are no longer the setup path. The limits chapter (Limits, CLIProxyAPI and fallbacks) also predates the current advice: keep each machine signed in to one account per provider, and add a machine for more capacity instead of switching subscriptions on one.

tutorials.title: Start SpecWithCode with a coordinator and two workers
tutorials.seoTitle: Start SpecWithCode: add a project, ask the coordinator, and watch two workers report back
tutorials.summary: A real run of SpecWithCode 1.0.45 on a sample repo: Settings shows the version, the plus next to Projects adopts the greet-app folder, and one request to the coordinator starts two Codex workers in parallel. They appear in the right panel, each finishes its SpecWeave task and ends with a report card saved in the increment, and the plan chip shows both tasks done and both acceptance criteria met.
tutorials.outcome: You end with a project whose coordinator has started two workers and returned a report.
prerequisites: a signed-in coding agent (Codex in this video)
a git repository, ideally with a SpecWeave increment planned

chapters.title: Two workers in the right panel

steps: Check your version in Settings, General, About.
Click the plus next to Projects. New project starts one from a name; Local folder adopts a repo you already have. The project opens on its coordinator.

Choose the project's permissions in the composer (Full access in this video); the choice applies to every chat in the project. Then ask the coordinator for the work: it does none of it itself, it starts worker threads and briefs each one with your words.
Watch the workers in the right panel, grouped as Waiting on you, Working, Idle and Resolved. They share one checkout, so give each its own files.
Open a worker. A final message with three headed sections becomes a report card, saved in the increment's reports folder; Open report reads it in full.

Click the plan chip to see the increment's tasks and acceptance criteria, with Open spec and Open increment. Put the increment number in each worker's title (for example `0001 T-01`): in 1.0.45 a worker's chip finds its increment only by title.
tutorials.note: Recorded headlessly in one take on a private SpecWithCode 1.0.45 server with a disposable home and a sample repo, 18 October 2026. Codex was the coordinator and both workers, signed in with the author's account through a short-lived token copied into that home; Claude Code is not installed there. Off camera, increment 0001 was planned in advance and the welcome wizard and a Codex update notice were dismissed. The permissions menu does not render in headless capture, so only its label changing to Full access is shown; Full access was chosen for the demo only. Known issues in 1.0.45, framed out of the video or noted on screen: the coordinator's worker cards can name the wrong task or lag behind the right panel, empty assistant headers appear in the coordinator timeline after workers finish, a worker's changed-files card also counts the other worker's edits, and a worker's own SpecWeave claim does not bind its plan chip, so only the title match works. Agent work is sped up where the video says so, and one permission moment is slowed to 0.5x. Narration is an AI voice (ElevenLabs, the author's cloned voice); captions are timed from the voice service's character timestamps.

tutorials.title: Keep working when a provider runs out
tutorials.seoTitle: Keep working when Claude Code hits its usage limit: SpecWithCode continues the thread on Codex
tutorials.summary: A real run of SpecWithCode 1.0.43 on a sample repo. A thread on Claude Code has finished T-01 of the increment. The next request stops on a usage limit, simulated with the app's documented test switch. Under the project's default rule, Switch automatically, SpecWithCode hands the stopped turn to Codex with its context, in the same worktree, and Codex finishes T-02. The SpecWeave ledger then shows who did each task, and Project settings, Usage limits, shows where to choose the rule. The video also shows a known issue in this build: after the switch, the model picker returns to Claude Code.
tutorials.outcome: You end with a thread that continued on another provider under a rule you set for the project.
prerequisites: two signed-in coding agents (Claude Code and Codex in this video)
a git repository with a SpecWeave increment planned

chapters.title: Claude Code hits its usage limit

steps: Open the thread in the project's right panel. Here it runs on Claude Code and has finished `T-01` of increment 0001.

Send the next request. When the provider stops on its usage limit, the thread shows a Usage limit reached banner with the reset time and what the project rule will do, for example Continuing with Codex by project rule.

Under the default rule, Switch automatically, SpecWithCode hands the stopped turn to Codex with its context, in the same worktree. The thread shows Context handoff and Claude Code limit reached, continued on Codex. The warning row then reads Usage limit resolved — chat continued: that means this chat continued, not that Claude Code's limit has reset.

Before you send the next message, check the composer's model picker. In SpecWithCode 1.0.43 it returns to Claude Code a few seconds after the switched turn ends, so the next message would go to Claude Code, stop on the limit and hand off again.
Run `specweave task list` in the repo. The By column shows which agent finished each task, with the test run that proved it, and `git log --oneline` shows both agents' commits.

Choose the rule in Project settings, Usage limits. When a provider runs out offers Switch automatically, Offer the fallback and Wait for the reset. With Offer the fallback, the thread waits until you click Continue with Codex.
Use Switch before the limit to move an idle thread early. The default is At 5% left.
tutorials.note: Recorded headlessly in one take on a private SpecWithCode 1.0.43 server with a disposable home and a sample repo, 18 October 2026. A real usage limit cannot be forced, so the limit is simulated with the app's documented test switch, STUDIO_SIMULATE_USAGE_LIMIT=claudeAgent, which makes every Claude Code turn stop with a limit that resets in one hour. T-01 was a real Claude Code turn, started off camera through the coordinator before the switch was turned on. T-02 was a real Codex turn, and the handoff, banner and ledger are the app's own. Both agents were signed in with the author's accounts through short-lived tokens copied into that home. Full access was chosen for the demo only. Nothing in Codex's turn is sped up; two still screens (the limit banner and the open plan list) play slower to fit the narration, and nothing moves in them. After the switch the composer's last frame is held for about 2 s, marked Still frame, and the walk to Project settings, Usage limits plays at 3×, marked Sped up 3×. The ledger beat is a captured terminal run of `specweave task list` and `git log --oneline -3`. Its first line, '0001-personal-greeting — agent cli@demo', is left out: cli@demo is the capture shell's own identity, not a third agent. Known issues in 1.0.43, shown in the video: the model picker returns to Claude Code after the automatic switch (the docs say it follows the switch), so the next message bounces back to Claude Code and hands off again; and the row 'Usage limit resolved — chat continued' does not mean Claude Code's limit has reset. Narration is an AI voice (ElevenLabs, the author's cloned voice); captions are timed from the voice service's character timestamps.

tutorials.title: Run a project with a coordinator and workers
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode projects: a Codex coordinator and a Claude worker
tutorials.summary: A Codex coordinator and a Claude worker in one project: model defaults, routing history, resolving and reopening threads, and token usage by model.
tutorials.outcome: You can tell the coordinator and worker models apart, follow the routing history, resolve and reopen a thread, and read token usage by model.
prerequisites: Claude Code and Codex signed in
steps: Set the coordinator and worker defaults separately. Existing threads keep their own model choices.
Talk to the coordinator. Its conversation stays in the project and keeps the routing history.
Open a worker thread on the right to see its details while the coordinator stays in view.
Choose Resolve when work is finished. History is kept, and Reopen brings the same thread back when related work returns.
Open Usage to compare coordinator and worker token totals by model. Cache reporting can be incomplete, and an API-equivalent cost is not money paid.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

tutorials.title: Plan, verify and schedule project work
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode plans and routines: verification receipts and scheduling
tutorials.summary: Write a short plan with one acceptance criterion, run a real verification that fails and then passes, and keep routines scoped to their project.
tutorials.outcome: You add a plan with one acceptance criterion, see a failed verification stay failed, record a passing attempt, and keep routines scoped to their project.
steps: Add a plan when acceptance needs evidence: a short spec, one acceptance criterion and a task. Ordinary chat does not need one.
Review the executable and its literal arguments before saving the verification command. Saving does not run it.
Run verification. A nonzero exit stays failed, and that receipt is kept unchanged.
Fix the cause, then choose a new attempt. The new receipt records the successful exit; Recheck reads the same receipt without running it again.
If the repository already has a SpecWeave ledger, it stays authoritative.
Routines keep their project and host. Pause the project to refuse new work; a turn already running is not killed.
Deleting a project needs its exact name and leaves its source folder intact.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

tutorials.title: Keep project memory and read honest usage
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode project memory and usage from recorded turns
tutorials.summary: Keep a project's goal, instructions and durable decisions in small memory files, then read usage that comes only from recorded provider turns.
tutorials.outcome: You keep a project goal, instructions and decisions in small memory files and read usage that comes only from recorded provider turns.
steps: Keep the project goal, instructions and durable facts together. Instructions guide future turns; they do not replace a provider’s own history.
Give a lasting decision its own small Markdown file and save it. SpecWithCode checks the file revision before replacing it.
Reload and reopen the file to confirm the decision persisted. Another project keeps its own memory.
Read usage, which comes from recorded provider turns. Missing data stays visible, and a cost estimate is not a bill.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

action.label: Read the memory and usage guide

tutorials.title: Continue a thread on Codex at a usage limit
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode tour: coordinator, workers and continuing on Codex
tutorials.summary: A project coordinator splits work between Codex and Claude workers, the results come back to one conversation, and a Claude thread at its usage limit continues on Codex with its context.
tutorials.outcome: You see a coordinator split work between Codex and Claude, and a Claude thread at its limit continue on Codex with its context.

chapters.title: Each job gets the model that fits
Results come back to one conversation
Hit a limit, continue on Codex

steps: Give the coordinator a goal. It starts a worker for each part and lists them with the threads.
Each job gets the model that fits: in the recording, Codex writes tip.py while Claude writes the README.
Results come back to one conversation, where the coordinator checks each worker’s output against the goal.
When Claude runs out, Continue with Codex carries the conversation over.
tutorials.note: Screen recordings on a Mac, 10 October 2026. No sound; the usage limit in the handoff clip is simulated. Recorded before SpecWithCode 1.0.0, so some labels have changed.

tutorials.title: Set up a personal project with folders and tools
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode personal projects, folders, repositories and MCP tools
tutorials.summary: A Personal project with app-managed storage: add a folder, link a repository, discover a local MCP command and grant exactly the tools it may use.
tutorials.outcome: You create a personal project, add a folder and a repository, and grant a local MCP command exactly the tools it may use.
steps: Start a Personal project. It uses app-managed storage on its device and needs no Git repository.
Add an existing folder and save its access grant. The folder is not moved.
Add a repository URL and associate your local checkout. Match checks the checkout’s actual remote.
Save a local MCP command, then choose Check to discover its tools. Check does not verify an external account.
Grant exactly the tools this project may use. Revoke removes future access; restoring needs a new check and new grants.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

tutorials.title: Check what an agent actually did
tutorials.seoTitle: Read an agent result in SpecWithCode: tool output, exit code and diff
tutorials.summary: Ask the agent for the result, inspect the recorded tool call and its exit code, review the file change, and preview the provider-switch warning.
tutorials.outcome: You can find the recorded tool call, its exit code and the file change behind an agent’s answer.

chapters.title: Ask the agent for the result

steps: Ask the agent for the result.
Expand the recorded work to see the actual tool and its output. The recorded command returned exit code 0.
Inspect the recorded file change.
Before switching providers, read the warning: prompt caches and runtime state do not transfer, and the portable chat context does.
tutorials.note: Actual browser recording of a synthetic task completed on 7 October 2026 in a disposable repository. The model-switching scene previews the confirmation UI in an isolated fixture.

tutorials.title: Run your first task with Claude Code
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode with Claude Code: plan, build and review one task
tutorials.summary: Set up SpecWithCode with Claude Code, run one real task through a project, and review the result.
tutorials.outcome: You end with Claude Code having planned, built and tested one change in your repository, with the ledger line that records who finished it.
steps: In your repository, run `specweave init`. It adds AGENTS.md and the SpecWeave skills.
Open SpecWithCode. In setup, keep this computer and choose Continue. The Claude card should say Ready to code; if it does not, run `claude auth login` in a terminal first.
Add the repository: choose the plus next to Projects, then Local folder, then its path. A new chat opens.
Pick Claude Code in the model picker. The recording sets Full access for the demo only.
Type `$`, pick `sw-increment` and describe the change. The agent writes spec.md with acceptance criteria and a task with its files and test.
Send `sw-do`. The agent claims the task, changes the code and runs the test. The task is marked done only when the test passes.
Choose Open diff to review the code, the test and the ledger line. Then `sw-done` verifies and closes the increment.

tutorials.title: Run your first task with Codex
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode with Codex: plan, build and review one task
tutorials.summary: Set up SpecWithCode with Codex, run one real task through a project, and review the result.
tutorials.outcome: You end with Codex having planned, built and tested one change in your repository, with the ledger line that records who finished it.
steps: In your repository, run `specweave init`. It adds AGENTS.md and the SpecWeave skills.
Open SpecWithCode. In setup, keep this computer and choose Continue. On the Codex card, choose Continue with ChatGPT, or run `codex login` and then Use existing CLI. The card says Ready to code.
Add the repository: choose the plus next to Projects, then Local folder, then its path. A new chat opens.
Pick Codex in the model picker. The recording sets Full access for the demo only.
Type `$`, pick `sw-increment` and describe the change. The agent writes spec.md with acceptance criteria and a task with its files and test.
Send `sw-do`. The agent claims the task, changes the code and runs the test. The task is marked done only when the test passes.
Choose Open diff to review the code, the test and the ledger line. Then `sw-done` verifies and closes the increment.

steps: In your repository, run `specweave init` with the generic adapter. It adds AGENTS.md and the SpecWeave skills.
In the repository, run `grok --trust` once, because Grok skips project skills in folders it does not trust. If you are signed out, run `grok login` first.
Open SpecWithCode, then Settings, Providers. Grok is off by default: choose Add provider, pick Grok and existing CLI, choose Next twice, then Add instance.
Add the repository: choose the plus next to Projects, then Local folder, then its path. A new chat opens.
Pick Grok in the model picker. The recording sets Full access for the demo only.
Type `$`, pick `sw-increment` and describe the change. The agent writes spec.md with acceptance criteria and a task with its files and test.
Send `sw-do`. The agent claims the task, changes the code and runs the test. The task is marked done only when the test passes.
Choose Open diff to review the code, the test and the ledger line. Then `sw-done` verifies and closes the increment.
